stories.headline: Romania shoots down a drone for the first time

sources.title: Romanian F-16 shoots down drone after airspace breach, marking first for NATO ally
F-16 downs drone in Romania's airspace for first time

chunks.text: A Romanian air force F-16 {{shot down}} a drone over Buzau County on Friday, July 24. Radar {{picked up}} the aircraft at 9:39 a.m., about 20 kilometers east of Sulina, and the pilot destroyed it with a missile at 11:02 a.m. The drone {{came down}} near the village of Padina. Foreign Minister Oana Toiu said it was the first time a drone had been intercepted and destroyed inside Romania's national airspace.

chunks.text: The lights {{went out}} across the whole of Georgia at about 00:10 on July 24. Tbilisi, Kutaisi and the breakaway region of Abkhazia all lost power [[at once]]. Georgian State Electrosystem, the national grid operator, said an emergency shutdown had caused it and that supply would return [[in stages]]. Power was fully restored at about 09:30, more than nine hours later, but the official cause is still unknown.

chunks.text: Japan's newest refrigerator is built for people. The Do Hiemon Box is a booth the size of a vending machine. One person steps inside, and air at 41 degrees Fahrenheit blows onto the head, neck, shoulders and back. After 20 minutes the machine {{shuts itself off}}. One of the first units has gone to Maebashi City Hall in Gunma Prefecture, where anyone can {{drop in}} and use it free during opening hours.

chunks.text: Hot nights are costing the average person about 56 hours of sleep a year, [[close to]] seven nights' worth, according to an analysis of 1,338 cities published on July 15 by the research group Climate Central. [[Roughly]] six of those hours, about one night, {{come down to}} human-caused warming. That [[share]] has [[at least]] doubled since the early 1970s, and it is far larger in some regions than others.

chunks.text: Heat {{keeps people up}} for a simple reason. Sleep depends on the body's ability to cool itself, and warm night air {{slows that cooling down}}. [[Rather than]] measure bedrooms, the team applied each city's lowest overnight temperature to a relationship between heat and sleep that an earlier study had [[established]], using data from nearly 50,000 people wearing sleep trackers. Kelton Minor of the University of Copenhagen, who led that study, said, "The warmer it gets, the less that people sleep."

chunks.text: People in parts of southern India and Southeast Asia lose 78 to 91 hours a year to warm nights, against 36 hours across 253 US cities. Chennai loses more than any other Indian city, 93 hours. The team was [[open about]] one [[weakness]]: the sleep research behind its model was based mostly on people in higher-[[income]] countries, where cooling is easier to {{come by}}, so losses in poorer places may be bigger than these [[figures]] [[suggest]].

chunks.text: Scientists have {{found out}} that giraffes can do simple math. Researchers at the University of Barcelona {{carried out}} a study with four giraffes at a zoo in Spain. They wanted to see [[whether]] the animals could {{work out}} which amount of food was bigger. The results [[surprised]] many people.

chunks.text: In the test, the scientists {{set up}} clear containers with different numbers of carrot and vegetable pieces. Sometimes they added more pieces, and sometimes they {{took away}} a few. Each time, the giraffes had to {{pick out}} the container with more food. To get the reward, the animals used their long tongues to reach it.

chunks.text: When the scientists added pieces, the giraffes did [[far better]] than [[luck]] alone would explain. According to the study, they chose the larger amount about 68 percent of the time. This helped the team {{rule out}} the idea that the animals were only [[guessing]]. The results [[suggest]] giraffes can {{keep track of}} small numbers and can {{tell apart}} large and small amounts of food. However, the animals could not [[solve]] harder tasks, [[such as]] subtraction.

chunks.text: For a long time, people thought that only humans and a few clever animals, such as primates and crows, had [[a sense of]] numbers. This new study adds to [[a growing list]] of animals that can count [[in some way]]. The researchers now want to {{carry on}} their work with other zoo animals. They hope it will help us {{figure out}} more about how animal minds work.

tf.s: Researchers carried on a new study with four giraffes at a zoo in Spain.
tf.why: The researchers carried out (performed) a new study. Carry on means to continue something that is already happening.

tf.s: In the test, the giraffes had to pick out the container that held more food.
tf.why: Each time, the giraffes had to pick out (choose) the container with more food to get the reward.

tf.s: Sometimes the scientists picked out a few pieces of food from the containers.
tf.why: Sometimes the scientists took away (removed) a few pieces. Pick out means to choose one thing from several, not to remove one.

tf.s: Scientists found out that giraffes can do simple math.
tf.why: Researchers at the University of Barcelona found out (discovered) that giraffes can do simple math.

tf.s: The researchers want to carry on their work with other zoo animals.
tf.why: The team wants to carry on (continue) their research to learn more about how animal minds work.

tf.s: This new study takes away from the growing list of animals that can count in some way.
tf.why: The study adds to (makes bigger) the growing list of animals that can count. Take away from means to make smaller, the opposite.
